questions.q: Put the asset lifecycle stages in the correct order.
options: Retirement, Addition, Depreciation, Adjustment, In Service
Addition, In Service, Depreciation, Adjustment/Transfer, Retirement
Depreciation, Retirement, Addition, Adjustment, In Service
In Service, Retirement, Addition, Depreciation, Adjustment
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs addition, then capitalization/in service, then depreciation, then adjustments or transfers while in use, then retirement.

questions.q: Which real business need does accurate asset location data support?
options: Property tax reporting and physical inventory audits
Setting the General Ledger's functional currency
Determining a vendor's payment terms
Calculating sales tax on customer invoices
questions.explain: Location data is used to file property tax correctly by jurisdiction and to verify, during a physical audit, that assets are actually where the books say.

questions.q: Which book class is used first for every new asset?
options: Tax book
Budget book
Corporate book
None — assets don't need a book until retirement
questions.explain: Every asset starts life in a corporate book, the primary book used for financial statement reporting.

questions.q: Does the depreciation calendar have to be identical to the General Ledger's accounting calendar?
options: Yes, Oracle Fusion Assets requires them to be identical
No, they can differ, though many implementations align them to simplify reconciliation
No, and aligning them is never recommended
Depreciation calendars were replaced by prorate calendars in Fusion
questions.explain: The depreciation calendar is a separate structure from the GL calendar; they don't have to match, though keeping them aligned simplifies later reconciliation work.

questions.q: Which depreciation method type looks up a predefined rate using an asset's life and year of life, rather than calculating a fresh formula each period?
options: Calculated (straight-line)
Table-based
Units of production
Flat-rate
questions.explain: Table-based methods pull a published rate from a table based on life and year of life — how many accelerated tax schedules like MACRS are implemented.

questions.q: Why do many implementations align the depreciation calendar's period naming with the GL calendar even though the two are technically independent structures?
options: Oracle Fusion requires them to use identical names
It makes later reconciliation between Assets and GL easier
It is required for depreciation to calculate at all
It prevents tax books from being created
questions.explain: Aligning period naming conventions between the depreciation calendar and the GL calendar simplifies reconciliation work later, even though the calendars are independent structures.

questions.q: What does a queue status of ON HOLD mean for a mass addition line?
options: It has already become a posted asset
It is flagged for review and not yet ready to post
It was deleted and will never become an asset
It was merged into another asset
questions.explain: ON HOLD means the line needs further review or missing information before it can be marked ready to post.

questions.q: Which information group includes the date placed in service?
options: Assignment information
Financial information
Location information
Category description only
questions.explain: Financial information includes cost, units, book assignment, and the date placed in service.

questions.q: What queue status does a line carry after it has successfully posted?
options: NEW
ON HOLD
POSTED
DELETE
questions.explain: Once Post Mass Additions successfully processes a line, its status changes to POSTED and it becomes a real row in the asset tables.

questions.q: Why do companies typically apply revaluation consistently across an entire category rather than selectively to individual assets?
options: To avoid distorting comparisons within the same asset population
Because Oracle Fusion Assets technically cannot revalue a single asset
Because revaluation is required to be applied to retired assets only
Because categories cannot contain more than one revalued asset
questions.explain: Applying revaluation consistently across a category or class of assets avoids distorting comparisons between assets that should be treated similarly.

questions.q: When is an asset considered impaired?
options: When its carrying amount is lower than its recoverable amount
When its recoverable amount is less than its carrying amount
When it is placed in service
When it is reclassified into a different category
questions.explain: An asset is impaired when its recoverable amount falls below its current carrying amount (net book value).

questions.q: Why is it standard practice to run preview mode before final mode?
options: Preview mode is required by law in all jurisdictions
Because final mode does not calculate correctly without a prior preview run
Because final mode closes the period, and closed periods generally can't be reopened, so errors should be caught beforehand
Preview mode is only available once per fiscal year
questions.explain: Since final mode closes the period and closed periods generally can't be reopened, reviewing preview results first lets errors be caught and fixed before committing.

questions.q: A company consistently depreciates its assets too slowly relative to their real decline in value. What pattern would this tend to produce at retirement?
options: Consistent gains on retirement
Consistent losses on retirement
No effect on gain/loss outcomes
Automatic reinstatement of all retired assets
questions.explain: Under-depreciating relative to real value decline leaves net book value too high, which tends to produce losses when the asset is actually retired for its true, lower value.

questions.q: What happens to the remaining units after a partial retirement?
options: They are automatically retired too
They continue depreciating normally, based on the reduced cost basis
They stop depreciating until the full asset is retired
They are transferred to a different book
questions.explain: In a partial retirement, only the retired portion leaves service; the remaining units keep depreciating on the asset's new, reduced cost basis.

questions.q: Why do mass transactions exist rather than requiring every asset to be processed individually?
options: Because individual transactions are not supported at all
Because mass transactions are required for all new asset additions
Because individual transactions do not calculate gain or loss
Because many real-world events affect many assets at once, and processing them individually is slow and risks inconsistency
questions.explain: Events like a warehouse closure or product discontinuation affect many assets simultaneously; mass transactions apply the same treatment consistently and efficiently.

questions.q: What is a tradeoff of transferring Fixed Assets journal entries to GL only at period end rather than more frequently?
options: There is no tradeoff; frequency never matters
GL's fixed-asset balances will lag behind what Assets shows throughout the month
Period-end-only transfer is always faster to process
Period-end-only transfer prevents any reconciliation from being possible
questions.explain: Transferring only at period end means GL's picture of fixed assets lags behind Assets' own data until the transfer runs, a deliberate tradeoff against more frequent processing.

questions.q: Which of these is a common timing-related cause of an apparent out-of-balance condition?
options: A category being too granular
A batch accounted in Assets but not yet transferred, or transferred but not yet posted in GL
An asset placed in service mid-year
A depreciation method using table-based rates
questions.explain: Timing gaps from the transfer-versus-post distinction (Lesson 29) are a very common and self-resolving cause of apparent discrepancies.

questions.q: What does the reserve ledger report show?
options: Future forecasted depreciation
Accumulated depreciation by asset
Only assets still in construction-in-process
Vendor payment history
questions.explain: The reserve ledger report ties to depreciation runs and adjustments, showing accumulated depreciation by asset.
